domain-modeling.responsibility: 为电商微服务系统进行领域建模，通过事件风暴识别限界上下文、核心事件、聚合根及上下文地图，为后续微服务拆分提供领域基础。
domain-modeling.implementation: 通常以事件风暴工作坊形式组织协作，先识别领域事件与命令，再聚合形成聚合根并划定限界上下文，最终输出上下文映射图与统一语言。
domain-modeling.design_intent: 在进入详细设计（尤其是订单的复杂状态机与分布式事务）之前，先把业务语义边界固化，避免按技术或数据表粒度误拆微服务，降低后续跨服务协作与一致性设计成本。
domain-modeling.constraints: 需覆盖用户、商品、订单、支付、库存、通知六大业务域；上下文划分须保持业务语义内聚、上下文间依赖清晰可治理；产出的事件与聚合根需支持后续订单状态机与分布式事务设计的可追溯性。

start.responsibility: Entry-point task that initiates the design of an e-commerce microservice backend covering user auth, product catalog, order processing, payment, inventory, and notifications on a Java + Spring Cloud Alibaba stack.
start.implementation: Carried out as a planning/root task: it frames the overall architecture, enumerates the bounded contexts to be designed, and sequences the design activities before drilling into domain-specific detail (notably the order-processing deep dive).
start.design_intent: Exists as the top-level scope anchor so that downstream design nodes (and the eventual deliverable) remain aligned with a single coherent backend vision rather than fragmented per-service designs.
start.constraints: Must cover all six listed sub-domains (auth, catalog, orders, payment, inventory, notifications); must respect the Java + Spring Cloud Alibaba stack choice; must treat order processing as the most complex area requiring state-machine and distributed-transaction handling; output feeds a single downstream deliverable node.

splitting-comparison.responsibility: Compare and contrast four candidate strategies for decomposing an e-commerce backend into microservices and recommend a preferred combination that fits the system's domains (auth, catalog, orders, payments, inventory, notifications).
splitting-comparison.implementation: Typically takes the form of a design-doc section that lays each candidate side-by-side against axes such as coupling, data ownership, transaction boundaries, team alignment, and operational complexity, then argues toward a hybrid recommendation rather than picking a single pure approach.
splitting-comparison.design_intent: Exists to make the upstream architecture decision explicit and traceable: by evaluating business-domain, user-journey, CQRS, and DDD-aggregate-root splits together, the document gives later design work (especially the detailed order-processing design) a defensible basis for service boundaries, ownership, and consistency strategy.
splitting-comparison.constraints: Must remain at the architectural-comparison level rather than re-deriving detailed mechanics of each style; the recommendation should be coherent with the rest of the e-commerce design (especially the order state machine and distributed-transaction needs) and should not contradict the chosen inter-service communication and data-consistency patterns used elsewhere in the project.

industry-practice.responsibility: Synthesize reusable architectural patterns from large-scale e-commerce platforms (Taobao/JD/Shopify) to inform the target microservice design's component choices and integration style.
industry-practice.implementation: Typically a written comparative analysis or reference section that maps common industry middleware (Nacos for discovery/config, Sentinel for flow control, Seata for distributed transactions, RocketMQ for async messaging) to the responsibilities of the target services such as order processing, inventory, and notifications.
industry-practice.design_intent: To anchor the proposed architecture in battle-tested patterns rather than reinventing primitives, reducing design risk for stateful concerns like the order state machine and distributed transactions, and to justify technology selection by precedent.
industry-practice.constraints: Must remain advisory rather than prescriptive on the target design; should call out patterns whose applicability depends on scale or team capability; should not lock the design into a single vendor stack without justification.

deliverable.responsibility: Produces the final design deliverables for an ecommerce microservice system: a high-level architecture overview document and an in-depth order-processing design covering state machine, distributed transaction handling, sequence flows, and fault tolerance.
deliverable.implementation: Realized as a design-document deliverable (likely a README and supporting sections within docs/design/ecommerce-microservice) that consolidates architectural decisions and detailed sub-designs into written artifacts rather than running code.
deliverable.design_intent: Serves as the terminal artifact of the design exercise — a reviewer-facing, navigable record of the proposed system so stakeholders can validate both the macroscopic service topology and the microscopic correctness of the most complex flow (order processing) before implementation begins.
deliverable.constraints: Must remain at design-document scope (no production code), must be self-consistent across the overview and the order-processing detail, must explicitly address the four flagged concerns (state machine correctness, distributed transaction semantics, sequencing, fault tolerance), and must be traceable back to the upstream planning task that initiates the workflow.

arch-plan.responsibility: Synthesize domain event storming results, candidate microservice decomposition options, and relevant industry best practices into a single architecture overview document that scopes the e-commerce backend.
arch-plan.implementation: Typically carried out as a planning artifact: gathering domain events from stakeholders, comparing service-split strategies (e.g., by subdomain vs. by business capability), and referencing established patterns for e-commerce backends before consolidating the chosen direction into an overview document.
arch-plan.design_intent: Exists as the top-of-funnel planning step that anchors all subsequent detailed design — particularly the complex order-processing design — by establishing shared vocabulary, service boundaries, and cross-cutting decisions up front.
arch-plan.constraints: Must cover all six named capability areas (auth, catalog, order with state machine and distributed transaction, payment, inventory sync, notifications); must be completed before detailed order-processing design begins; should remain at overview level and defer mechanism details to later nodes.
